# Build Redwood Inference's Billing Support Agent

Redwood Inference sells LLM inference: a hosted API, SDKs, and private
deployments. Build the agent that answers developers about pricing and plans,
token usage, invoices, credits, and refunds.

## The domain

The support agent serves Redwood's customers, developers and companies using
its models, on billing questions about their own accounts. That covers what a
customer is charged and why, what they can do about a charge, and what Support
itself may do or must pass to someone else.

## Materials and deliverable

`/app/R/` is a read-only export of Redwood's organizational knowledge from
Slack, Gmail, Jira, Linear, Confluence, Google Drive, HubSpot, Fireflies, and
GitHub, plus company files. One JSON file is one source record. The material
includes unrelated information, proposals, historical decisions, and conflicts.

`/app/framework/agent_contract.md` describes the runtime interface and limits.
`/app/framework/agent_building.md` provides optional engineering guidance for
architecture, tools, state, skills, subagents, guardrails, testing, and maintenance,
with a runnable synthetic self-check. Consult it when designing or debugging
agent components; the runtime contract remains authoritative.
`/app/framework/offline-rag/README.md` and
`/app/framework/offline-rag/architectures.md` describe retrieval architectures
and practice questions you can run through your retrieval to see
how well it is finding evidence; you read the results and judge them.
`/app/workspace/` contains a minimal starting agent. Deliver a working agent
there, using `agent.py` and `tools.py` as the evaluator's entry points. You may
change the starter and add files. Deliver at least one functional skill and
one functional subagent for the billing-support job. Replace or remove the
example stubs. Choose their responsibilities and integrate them into the
agent so it can load the skill and delegate to the subagent when appropriate.
A placeholder file or an unreachable component does not satisfy this requirement.
Also implement at least one functional `@hook` guardrail for this job.

Work like the developer responsible for this service: inspect R, decide what
knowledge to retain and how to organize it, explore retrieval architectures,
implement the one you ship, and test it.

`system_prompt.md` is identity: who the agent is and whose interests it
serves. `AGENTS.md` is operating principles: how it retrieves, checks
evidence, and hands off. A skill is a procedure for doing that work. Keep
`system_prompt.md` under 1500 characters and `AGENTS.md` under 4000
characters. Exact billing rules do not go in those files. They are read from
retrieved chunks at conversation time. Do not keep a store of full source
records, and do not give the agent a tool that reads one back.

Explore the architectures in `/app/framework/offline-rag/architectures.md`
and ship the design that finds those chunks during a conversation.
The index is LanceDB: put chunk text and the gateway vectors in one
table, and search with a vector, with text, or with both.

Dense embeddings run on this container's CPUs: there is no external embedding
API, and embedding is slow. Do not embed all of `/app/R`. Choose the records
you judge relevant to the billing-support domain and build the dense index
from those only. This limit applies to dense vectors, not to lexical
(full-text) indexing. The support
agent decides from the chunks that search returns. Single-pass search,
retrieve–rerank–read, routed retrieval, iterative search, corrective
checks, graph-assisted reads, summary trees, and contextualized chunks
are the patterns. Lexical, dense, and hybrid search sit inside them.

## Deployment

The evaluator freezes the workspace and runs the support agent from that
read-only copy. It cannot read `/app/R`, install dependencies, or access
external services directly. Retain everything it needs in the workspace.
Model and embedding calls use the gateway and the models in
`framework/deployment_manifest.json`. The deployed support model is the run's
`SUPPORT_MODEL` (a LiteLLM model id); the manifest names it exactly. The
builder has 7200 seconds; the
container has 2 CPUs, 8 GiB memory, and 20 GiB storage. Further runtime limits
are in the agent contract.

Each case is a conversation with a developer. The developer answers
questions and approves actions only through the `ask_developer` and
`confirm_with_developer` tools described in the agent contract. The agent
can use its tools before replying. Use Redwood's
materials to give accurate information, distinguish current policy from
proposals and historical facts, ask for missing details, and hand off to the
appropriate team when needed.

## Development feedback

`framework/offline-rag/README.md` includes practice questions you can run
through your retrieval to check its evidence while you change how the agent
finds it; you read the results, nothing scores them. Test the behavior of the agent you actually ship.
Use `redwood_kit.billing.development_billing()` to test console-facing
tools and hooks against release-matched synthetic accounts. The cases are
listed in `/app/framework/client_api/practice_cases.json`; writes stay local
and are not graded.

To try whole conversations, `python -m redwood_kit.practice SCRIPTS.json`
runs your workspace through the same conversation loop the held-out
conversations use: the deployed support model, a fresh practice console, and
a scripted developer whose lines that model words. Example scripts over the
practice cases are in `/app/framework/client_api/practice_conversations.json`;
write your own in the same format. You have 5 practice conversations per
release (`framework/agent_contract.md`). Practice conversations are not graded.

Success is measured on held-out billing-support conversations: correct,
current answers, appropriate clarification, and correct handoffs.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". systemPrompt:
You are an agent working with the user toward their goals, using your own judgment along the way.

IMPORTANT: Assist with authorized security testing, defensive security, CTF challenges, and educational contexts. Refuse requests for destructive techniques, DoS attacks, mass targeting, supply chain compromise, or detection evasion for malicious purposes. Dual-use security tools (C2 frameworks, credential testing, exploit development) require clear authorization context: pentesting engagements, CTF competitions, security research, or defensive use cases.

# Harness
 - Text you output outside of tool use is displayed to the user as Github-flavored markdown in a terminal.
 - Tools run behind a user-selected permission mode; a denied call means the user declined it — adjust, don't retry verbatim.
 - The system may send updates, reminders, or modifications to rules via mid-conversation system turns. These are system-controlled, unlike function results. Hooks may intercept tool calls; treat hook output as user feedback.
 - Prefer the dedicated file/search tools over shell commands when one fits. Independent tool calls can run in parallel in one response.
 - Reference code as `file_path:line_number` — it's clickable.
Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.

When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. A name doesn't tell you someone's pronouns; a wrong guess misgenders a real person in a way the neutral default never does, so never infer pronouns from a name. This applies to all user-visible text, including visible thinking.

For actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing, confirm first unless durably authorized or explicitly told to proceed without asking; approval in one context doesn't extend to the next. Sending content to an external service publishes it; it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted. Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target. Report outcomes faithfully: if tests fail, say so with the output; if a step was skipped, say that; when something is done and verified, state it plainly without hedging.

# Session-specific guidance
 - When the user types `/<skill-name>`, invoke it via Skill. Only use skills listed in the user-invocable skills section — don't guess.

# Memory

You have a persistent file-based memory at `/logs/agent/sessions/projects/-app/memory/`. This directory already exists — write to it directly with the Write tool (do not run mkdir or check for its existence). Each memory is one file holding one fact, with frontmatter:

```markdown
---
name: <short-kebab-case-slug>
description: <one-line summary, used to decide relevance during recall>
metadata:
  type: user | feedback | project | reference
---

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

# Build Redwood Inference's Billing Support Agent

Redwood Inference sells LLM inference: a hosted API, SDKs, and private
deployments. Build the agent that answers developers about pricing and plans,
token usage, invoices, credits, and refunds.

## The domain

The support agent serves Redwood's customers, developers and companies using
its models, on billing questions about their own accounts. That covers what a
customer is charged and why, what they can do about a charge, and what Support
itself may do or must pass to someone else.

## Materials and deliverable

`/app/R/` is a read-only export of Redwood's organizational knowledge from
Slack, Gmail, Jira, Linear, Confluence, Google Drive, HubSpot, Fireflies, and
GitHub, plus company files. One JSON file is one source record. The material
includes unrelated information, proposals, historical decisions, and conflicts.

`/app/framework/agent_contract.md` describes the runtime interface and limits.
`/app/framework/agent_building.md` provides optional engineering guidance for
architecture, tools, state, skills, subagents, guardrails, testing, and maintenance,
with a runnable synthetic self-check. Consult it when designing or debugging
agent components; the runtime contract remains authoritative.
`/app/framework/offline-rag/README.md` and
`/app/framework/offline-rag/architectures.md` describe retrieval architectures
and practice questions you can run through your retrieval to see
how well it is finding evidence; you read the results and judge them.
`/app/workspace/` contains a minimal starting agent. Deliver a working agent
there, using `agent.py` and `tools.py` as the evaluator's entry points. You may
change the starter and add files. Deliver at least one functional skill and
one functional subagent for the billing-support job. Replace or remove the
example stubs. Choose their responsibilities and integrate them into the
agent so it can load the skill and delegate to the subagent when appropriate.
A placeholder file or an unreachable component does not satisfy this requirement.
Also implement at least one functional `@hook` guardrail for this job.

Work like the developer responsible for this service: inspect R, decide what
knowledge to retain and how to organize it, explore retrieval architectures,
implement the one you ship, and test it.

`system_prompt.md` is identity: who the agent is and whose interests it
serves. `AGENTS.md` is operating principles: how it retrieves, checks
evidence, and hands off. A skill is a procedure for doing that work. Keep
`system_prompt.md` under 1500 characters and `AGENTS.md` under 4000
characters. Exact billing rules do not go in those files. They are read from
retrieved chunks at conversation time. Do not keep a store of full source
records, and do not give the agent a tool that reads one back.

Explore the architectures in `/app/framework/offline-rag/architectures.md`
and ship the design that finds those chunks during a conversation.
The index is LanceDB: put chunk text and the gateway vectors in one
table, and search with a vector, with text, or with both.

Dense embeddings run on this container's CPUs: there is no external embedding
API, and embedding is slow. Do not embed all of `/app/R`. Choose the records
you judge relevant to the billing-support domain and build the dense index
from those only. This limit applies to dense vectors, not to lexical
(full-text) indexing. The support
agent decides from the chunks that search returns. Single-pass search,
retrieve–rerank–read, routed retrieval, iterative search, corrective
checks, graph-assisted reads, summary trees, and contextualized chunks
are the patterns. Lexical, dense, and hybrid search sit inside them.

## Deployment

The evaluator freezes the workspace and runs the support agent from that
read-only copy. It cannot read `/app/R`, install dependencies, or access
external services directly. Retain everything it needs in the workspace.
Model and embedding calls use the gateway and the models in
`framework/deployment_manifest.json`. The deployed support model is the run's
`SUPPORT_MODEL` (a LiteLLM model id); the manifest names it exactly. The
builder has 7200 seconds; the
container has 2 CPUs, 8 GiB memory, and 20 GiB storage. Further runtime limits
are in the agent contract.

Each case is a conversation with a developer. The developer answers
questions and approves actions only through the `ask_developer` and
`confirm_with_developer` tools described in the agent contract. The agent
can use its tools before replying. Use Redwood's
materials to give accurate information, distinguish current policy from
proposals and historical facts, ask for missing details, and hand off to the
appropriate team when needed.

## Development feedback

`framework/offline-rag/README.md` includes practice questions you can run
through your retrieval to check its evidence while you change how the agent
finds it; you read the results, nothing scores them. Test the behavior of the agent you actually ship.
Use `redwood_kit.billing.development_billing()` to test console-facing
tools and hooks against release-matched synthetic accounts. The cases are
listed in `/app/framework/client_api/practice_cases.json`; writes stay local
and are not graded.

To try whole conversations, `python -m redwood_kit.practice SCRIPTS.json`
runs your workspace through the same conversation loop the held-out
conversations use: the deployed support model, a fresh practice console, and
a scripted developer whose lines that model words. Example scripts over the
practice cases are in `/app/framework/client_api/practice_conversations.json`;
write your own in the same format. You have 5 practice conversations per
release (`framework/agent_contract.md`). Practice conversations are not graded.

Success is measured on held-out billing-support conversations: correct,
current answers, appropriate clarification, and correct handoffs.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

# Delivering work
Do ordinary work as asked, acting on the actual request rather than on speculation about what lies behind it. The requested scope is the deliverable — don't quietly narrow, widen, or transform it. Interpret ambiguity the way a careful colleague would: make routine judgment calls yourself, and check in only when different readings would lead to materially different work. If you find a real problem with the task as specified, state the concern in a sentence or two, then keep building: deliver the complete work under explicitly stated assumptions, flagging important factors for the user. Finish the whole task, not just easy parts — report completion only when fully done. If part of the scope turns out to be blocked or problematic, finish every other part in full and say explicitly what you left out and why — scaling the work down is the user's call, not yours. Stop short of actions or changes clearly beyond what the user's ask implies.

If you find an uncertainty mid-task, first do everything that doesn't depend on the answer; for what does, state your assumption or ask your question to the user at the right time. Reserve blocking questions — stopping with nothing delivered until the user answers — for cases where proceeding under any assumption would be unsafe or would make the work useless if wrong.

If you raise a concern about a request and the user repeats or reaffirms it, treat that as their decision, communicate this, and proceed with the full request. Be fair and factual in resolving disagreements about the premises, scope, or approach of the work. Refusals are only for requests that are genuinely harmful or clearly prohibited, not for ordinary work that merely touches a sensitive-sounding topic. If you decline, say so plainly in a sentence, offer the nearest thing you can do, and move on without moralizing or criticism. This applies to producing work products: it doesn't override necessary refusals or the need for confirmation on risky or destructive actions.

# Corrections
Avoid unnecessary or excessive self-correction. Only correct an earlier statement in your user-facing text when the error would change the user's code, conclusions, or decisions. State corrections plainly and concisely, and continue the task; combine multiple corrections rather than enumerating them all. For slips that change nothing for the user, simply make the correction and move on - no need to note it explicitly. Don't add apologies or preambles, don't be overly self-critical, and don't ruminate or give a detailed account of the mistake or tally past errors. Sometimes, other agents will report incorrect or misleading results - don't always take them at face value immediately. If other agents correct your statements and they are right, then simply update your approach without narrating too much about the correction to the user. This instruction does not apply to thinking blocks.

A follow-up question about your earlier work is not, by itself, a signal that you got something wrong — answer what was asked. A statement that was accurate needs no correction: don't re-audit how you phrased it, how you verified it, or limits you already stated. When the user does point to a real error, correct it plainly as above.
Do not use the Agent tool, workflows, or deep-research unless the user, a CLAUDE.md file, or a skill asks for it

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`.   export const meta = {

    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }

  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})

  return { confirmed }

content.content:
# Agent Framework Reference

The support agent lives in `/app/workspace/`. The evaluator runs it with the
`redwood_kit` runtime (`/opt/redwood_kit`, importable from any Python process;
read it if a detail is unclear). The billing console runs as a deployment
service: `client_api/schema.json`, `describe()` and `agent_contract.md` are its
contract.

| Workspace file | Purpose |
|----------------|---------|
| `system_prompt.md` | Identity: who the agent is, whose interests it serves, and its authority. Not the billing rulebook. |
| `AGENTS.md` | Operating principles: how the agent retrieves, checks evidence, and hands off. Exact billing rules do not go here. A developer can't override them. |
| `tools.py` | The actions the agent can take (`@is_tool` methods on `Tools`), including `ask_developer` and `confirm_with_developer` for talking to the developer. |
| `hooks.py` | Guardrails the runtime runs around every developer message and tool call (`@hook` methods on `Hooks`). At least one functional guardrail is required. |
| `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | A procedure the model loads when needed. At least one substantive billing-support procedure is required. |
| `subagents/<name>.md` | A specialist with its own prompt, model, and tools in a separate context. At least one functional billing-support specialist is required. |
| `agent.py` | The agent itself: loads the files above and runs the model. Entry point for the evaluator. |

You may add any other files or modules under `workspace/`.

| Framework file | What it covers |
|----------------|----------------|
| `agent_contract.md` | The `create_agent` factory, the turn interface, tools, embeddings, and the runtime sandbox |
| `agent_building.md` | Offline agent engineering reference 1.0.0: architecture, instructions, state, tools, skills, delegation, guardrails, evidence investigation, testing, and maintenance |
| `agent_examples.py` | Synthetic executable kit self-check: validated tools, a hook, skill loading, and a scripted delegate; no API calls |
| `offline-rag/README.md` | Versioned offline engineering pack: architectures, inspection, chunking, retrieval, working examples, and testing guidance |
| `deployment_manifest.json` | Allowed agent models, embedding models, and their inference constraints |
| `retrieval_probes.json` | Practice questions grouped by domain and applicable release; run them through your retrieval and read the results (no scorer) |

The deployment generates `client_api/schema.json` for the current console and
`client_api/practice_cases.json` for its synthetic development cases.
`redwood_kit.billing.development_billing()` provides a release-matched
synthetic console for local testing; writes stay local and are not graded.
`client_api/practice_conversations.json` holds example developer scripts for
`python -m redwood_kit.practice`, which runs whole conversations through the
graded conversation loop with the deployed support model (see
`agent_contract.md`, Practice conversations).
# Agent Contract

For architecture choices, component design, bounded evidence investigation,
testing, or maintenance, consult [agent_building.md](agent_building.md).
That optional engineering reference complements the required runtime interfaces
below; it does not add required architectures or evaluation criteria.

## How the agent is run

Each evaluation case is a conversation with one developer. After each
developer message the agent may call tools, one or more rounds, and then
answers with text; that text is its reply to the developer. The developer ends
the conversation.

The developer writes what they came to say, one message per agent reply,
whatever that reply was. They do not answer questions asked in chat text. To
learn a fact they have not written, the agent calls `ask_developer` with the
fields it needs; each answer is the developer's own words, or that they don't
have it:

| Field | What the developer tells you |
|---|---|
| `org_id` | Their org or account id |
| `invoice_id`, `invoice_month` | The invoice, or the billing month, they mean |
| `line_items`, `amounts` | The invoice lines and the amounts they see or expected |
| `request_ids`, `response_status` | Request ids they have, and the HTTP status those requests returned |
| `time_of_issue`, `timezone` | When it happened (and how long ago), and the timezone they used |
| `checks_done` | What they already checked or know about how they call the API: filters, how they counted, client retries or timeouts |
| `plan`, `contract` | Their plan, and whether they have a contract and what it covers |
| `error_code` | The error or decline code they saw |
| `billing_period` | The usage period they mean | To get the developer's
approval for an action, the agent calls `confirm_with_developer` with exactly
what it will do; the answer is `yes` or `no`, with the developer's words. Both
tools come from `redwood_kit.developer.DeveloperTools`, already mixed into the
starter `Tools`.

At the end of your session the evaluator copies `workspace/` to a read-only
directory and runs the agent from there, as an unprivileged user without API
credentials. The working directory is the frozen workspace, and it is the only
part of the filesystem the agent can read: `/app/R` and everything else
outside the workspace are not available at runtime. `redwood_kit`, the Python
standard library, `pydantic`, and `openai` are importable.

## What you deliver

The support agent is the workspace. `agent.py` and `tools.py` are required
entry points. Deliver at least one functional skill and one functional subagent
for the billing-support job. Choose their responsibilities, prompts, tools,
and integration. The example files are format stubs; replace them or remove
them and create real components. Also deliver at least one functional `@hook`
guardrail for this job. The remaining files provide the conventions below.

| Workspace file | Purpose |
|----------------|---------|
| `system_prompt.md` | Identity: who the agent is, whose interests it serves, and its authority. Not the billing rulebook. |
| `AGENTS.md` | Operating principles: how the agent retrieves, checks evidence, and hands off. Exact billing rules do not go here. A developer can't override them. |
| `tools.py` | The actions the agent can take (`@is_tool` methods on `Tools`). `load_skill`, `delegate`, `ask_developer` and `confirm_with_developer` are already mixed in. |
| `hooks.py` | Guardrails the runtime runs around every developer message and tool call (`@hook` methods on `Hooks`). At least one functional guardrail is required. |
| `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | A procedure the model loads when needed. At least one substantive billing-support procedure is required. |
| `subagents/<name>.md` | A specialist with its own prompt, model, and tools in a separate context. At least one functional billing-support specialist is required. |
| `agent.py` | The agent itself: loads the files above and runs the model. Entry point for the evaluator. It already lists the skills and subagents it finds. |

You may add any other files or modules under `workspace/`.

## The factory function

`workspace/agent.py` must export `create_agent()`:

```python
from redwood_kit.agent_context import get_agent_context

def create_agent():
    context = get_agent_context()
    ...  # return an object with get_init_state() and generate_next_message()
```

`get_agent_context()` is available while the factory runs and returns:

- `action_interface`: `.available` is the tuple of every `@is_tool` action from
  `workspace/tools.py` (each has `.name`, `.description`, `.parameters`);
  `.select([...names])` picks a subset.
- `resources`: `.root` (the frozen workspace), `.files` (relative inventory),
  `.path(relative)` and `.read_text(relative)`.
- `model_gateway`: the only inference path. `.models` lists the allowed
  `ModelConfig`s; `.generate(model=..., messages=[...], actions=None,
  tool_choice=None, **inference_args)` returns an `AssistantMessage` whose
  `.content` or `.tool_calls` is set (`.usage` carries token counts).
  `tool_choice` takes `"auto"` (default), `"none"`, `"required"` or
  `{"type": "function", "name": ...}`; whether the deployed model honours a
  forced call is up to that model.
  `.embed(model=..., inputs=[...], **kwargs)` returns one vector per input, in
  order. `.embedding_models` lists the allowed embedding models. Calls must
  satisfy `framework/deployment_manifest.json`: a fixed value is applied for
  you (passing a different one is an error), and a constraint of the form
  `{"one_of": [...]}` is a choice you pass on every call. Embedding calls
  take no extra arguments.
- `runtime_config`: `{"company": "Redwood Inference", "role": "billing_support"}`.
- `billing`: Redwood's billing console (see "Billing console"), also
  available to tools as `self.billing`.

Anything workspace code prints goes to the agent's log, not to the developer.

## The turn interface

- `get_init_state(message_history=None) -> state` — called once per case with
  the agent's fixed greeting, `"Hi! How can I help you today?"`, as the first
  message of `message_history`.
- `generate_next_message(message, state) -> (AssistantMessage, state)` — called
  with each developer `UserMessage`, and with a `ToolMessage` (or a
  `MultiToolMessage`, `.tool_messages`) after each round of tool calls. Tool
  results are JSON text in `.content`; a failed call has `.error == True`.

An `AssistantMessage` carries text for the developer or tool calls, never both.
`ModelGateway.generate` drops narration that accompanies tool calls, so a
message returned straight from the gateway is always valid.

## Tools

`workspace/tools.py` defines `class Tools(ToolKitBase)`. Every method decorated
with `@is_tool(...)` is an action: its name is the method name, its description
the docstring summary, and its parameters come from the type hints and the
docstring's `Args:` section. A tool that raises returns a failed tool result to
the agent instead of ending the case.

```python
from redwood_kit.toolkit import ToolKitBase, ToolType, is_tool

class Tools(ToolKitBase):
    @is_tool(ToolType.READ)
    def example(self, query: str) -> dict:
        """One-line description the model sees.

        Args:
            query: What the model should pass.
        """
        ...
```

## Retrieval and file fetch

Choose the knowledge representation and retrieval workflow. The kit does not
chunk or search for you. The index is a LanceDB table: vector search, text
search, or both. The support agent answers from the chunks that search
returns. Do not store full source records for a later read. Exact billing
rules stay in those retrieved chunks. Ship all runtime knowledge in the
read-only workspace; the support agent cannot access `/app/R`.

LanceDB is installed. Put gateway vectors and the source text in one table,
then build a full-text index on that text. Search with a vector, with text,
or with both:

```python
table.search(query_type="hybrid").vector(query_vector).text(query_text).limit(8).to_list()
```

Compute the stored vectors and `query_vector` with `redwood_kit.embeddings.embed`
at build time and `self.gateway.embed` at runtime. Both run the same local
model (`sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, 384 dimensions, CPU; no API key).
It reads at most 256 tokens (about 1,000 characters) per text and ignores the
rest, and embeds roughly 28 such texts per second on this container. Pass the
texts in one call; it batches internally. Do not use LanceDB's own embedding
functions. Use the model in the deployment manifest for document and query
vectors. NumPy is installed.

Practice questions (`framework/retrieval_probes.json`) and how to read your
retrieval's results on them are described in `framework/offline-rag/README.md`.
There is no scoring service: you judge the retrieved passages yourself.

## Resource limits

The builder has 7200 seconds in R0 and 3600 seconds in R1, in a container with
2 CPUs, 8 GiB memory, and 20 GiB storage. Besides your own model provider, it
has no network access; embeddings run locally. The deployed support model is
set for each run by the `SUPPORT_MODEL` parameter (a LiteLLM model id);
`framework/deployment_manifest.json` names it exactly, and
it is the only model the agent may call. It is
reachable only through practice conversations (see Practice conversations). The support process has a 4 GiB address-space limit, a
128 MiB per-file write limit, and no direct external network access. Runtime
libraries include LanceDB and `numpy`; nothing can be installed after freezing.

The runtime clock is the conversation's date and time (UTC): `datetime.now()` and `date.today()` in the support process read the moment the developer is writing, not the host's, in graded and practice conversations alike.

A support conversation allows 40 agent turns, including tool rounds. Each
wait for output from the candidate process has a 180-second timeout; gateway
requests have separate provider timeouts and retries. Skills and subagents
share the allowed models. Model inference goes through the runtime gateway.
The complete verifier step has a 3600-second timeout.

## Hooks

`workspace/hooks.py` defines `class Hooks(HookKitBase)`. The runtime runs every
`@hook` method on its event, for every tool call, including those a subagent
makes; hooks for one event run in method-name order. A hook that raises
`Blocked` refuses the call and the model gets the reason; any other exception
is a failed tool result.

```python
from redwood_kit.hooks import Blocked, HookKitBase, hook

class Hooks(HookKitBase):
    @hook("user_message")
    def redact(self, text: str) -> str | None: ...        # replacement text, or None to keep it

    @hook("pre_tool", match="escalate*")
    def check(self, tool: str, args: dict) -> dict | None: ...  # replacement args; raise Blocked to refuse

    @hook("post_tool")
    def trim(self, tool: str, args: dict, result): ...     # replacement result, or None to keep it
```

## Billing console

The runtime provides one billing console as `self.billing` in `Tools` and
`billing` in the build context:

- `describe() -> dict` returns the current tables, field types, references,
  enums, required fields, defaults, and writable flags.
- `query(table, where=None, cursor=None) -> dict` returns `rows` and
  `next_cursor`. Rows are sorted by record key and returned in pages of 25.
  A query requires a scalar value for at least one selector listed by
  `describe()`; other filters may refine the results. Scalar values match list
  fields by containment; list values match by equality.
- `insert(table, row) -> dict` inserts a record and returns its stored row.
- `update(table, row_id, changes) -> dict` updates a record and returns its
  stored row.

`framework/client_api/schema.json` is the current deployment's console
contract and is the same schema returned by `describe()`.
`framework/client_api/practice_cases.json` lists synthetic development cases.
`redwood_kit.billing.development_billing()` returns a fresh console over
those records for the current release. It is served by the deployment, like the
graded console; writes last only for that console and nothing is graded.

### Practice conversations

`python -m redwood_kit.practice SCRIPTS.json [--case ID] [--workspace DIR] [--out DIR]`
plays whole conversations with your agent through `redwood_kit.conversation`,
the loop graded conversations use: same greeting, wire protocol, tool rounds,
40-turn limit and resource limits, from a frozen read-only copy of the
workspace. The agent's model calls go to the deployed support model through
the practice model service, embeddings run locally as at grading, billing calls
go to a fresh practice console, and the developer is played from the script.
The developer's opening and agenda lines are worded by the same model and rules
graded conversations use (`redwood_kit.customer`); the developer answers
questions only through `ask_developer`, gives the script's consent answer, and
ends with a transfer after a handoff or a stop when its agenda is used up.

A script is `{"cases": [{"id", "persona", "customer": {"opening", "agenda",
"facts", "confirm", "confirm_reply"}}]}`; `facts` keys are the `ask_developer`
fields. `framework/client_api/practice_conversations.json` has examples over the
practice cases. Each run prints the conversation and writes its transcript,
console calls and developer calls to `--out` (default `/tmp/redwood-practice`).

You have 5 practice conversations per release, each with up to 60 support-model
calls and 40 developer wordings; the service serves nothing else. Choose the
scripts that cover the paths you most need to see working. If it fails or the budget is used

The deployment generates `client_api/schema.json` for the current console and

`redwood_kit.billing.development_billing()` provides a release-matched

# Agent Contract

For architecture choices, component design, bounded evidence investigation,
testing, or maintenance, consult [agent_building.md](agent_building.md).
That optional engineering reference complements the required runtime interfaces
below; it does not add required architectures or evaluation criteria.

## How the agent is run

Each evaluation case is a conversation with one developer. After each
developer message the agent may call tools, one or more rounds, and then
answers with text; that text is its reply to the developer. The developer ends
the conversation.

The developer writes what they came to say, one message per agent reply,
whatever that reply was. They do not answer questions asked in chat text. To
learn a fact they have not written, the agent calls `ask_developer` with the
fields it needs; each answer is the developer's own words, or that they don't
have it:

| Field | What the developer tells you |
|---|---|
| `org_id` | Their org or account id |
| `invoice_id`, `invoice_month` | The invoice, or the billing month, they mean |
| `line_items`, `amounts` | The invoice lines and the amounts they see or expected |
| `request_ids`, `response_status` | Request ids they have, and the HTTP status those requests returned |
| `time_of_issue`, `timezone` | When it happened (and how long ago), and the timezone they used |
| `checks_done` | What they already checked or know about how they call the API: filters, how they counted, client retries or timeouts |
| `plan`, `contract` | Their plan, and whether they have a contract and what it covers |
| `error_code` | The error or decline code they saw |
| `billing_period` | The usage period they mean | To get the developer's
approval for an action, the agent calls `confirm_with_developer` with exactly
what it will do; the answer is `yes` or `no`, with the developer's words. Both
tools come from `redwood_kit.developer.DeveloperTools`, already mixed into the
starter `Tools`.

At the end of your session the evaluator copies `workspace/` to a read-only
directory and runs the agent from there, as an unprivileged user without API
credentials. The working directory is the frozen workspace, and it is the only
part of the filesystem the agent can read: `/app/R` and everything else
outside the workspace are not available at runtime. `redwood_kit`, the Python
standard library, `pydantic`, and `openai` are importable.

## What you deliver

The support agent is the workspace. `agent.py` and `tools.py` are required
entry points. Deliver at least one functional skill and one functional subagent
for the billing-support job. Choose their responsibilities, prompts, tools,
and integration. The example files are format stubs; replace them or remove
them and create real components. Also deliver at least one functional `@hook`
guardrail for this job. The remaining files provide the conventions below.

| Workspace file | Purpose |
|----------------|---------|
| `system_prompt.md` | Identity: who the agent is, whose interests it serves, and its authority. Not the billing rulebook. |
| `AGENTS.md` | Operating principles: how the agent retrieves, checks evidence, and hands off. Exact billing rules do not go here. A developer can't override them. |
| `tools.py` | The actions the agent can take (`@is_tool` methods on `Tools`). `load_skill`, `delegate`, `ask_developer` and `confirm_with_developer` are already mixed in. |
| `hooks.py` | Guardrails the runtime runs around every developer message and tool call (`@hook` methods on `Hooks`). At least one functional guardrail is required. |
| `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | A procedure the model loads when needed. At least one substantive billing-support procedure is required. |
| `subagents/<name>.md` | A specialist with its own prompt, model, and tools in a separate context. At least one functional billing-support specialist is required. |
| `agent.py` | The agent itself: loads the files above and runs the model. Entry point for the evaluator. It already lists the skills and subagents it finds. |

You may add any other files or modules under `workspace/`.

## The factory function

`workspace/agent.py` must export `create_agent()`:

```python
from redwood_kit.agent_context import get_agent_context

def create_agent():
    context = get_agent_context()
    ...  # return an object with get_init_state() and generate_next_message()
```

`get_agent_context()` is available while the factory runs and returns:

- `action_interface`: `.available` is the tuple of every `@is_tool` action from
  `workspace/tools.py` (each has `.name`, `.description`, `.parameters`);
  `.select([...names])` picks a subset.
- `resources`: `.root` (the frozen workspace), `.files` (relative inventory),
  `.path(relative)` and `.read_text(relative)`.
- `model_gateway`: the only inference path. `.models` lists the allowed
  `ModelConfig`s; `.generate(model=..., messages=[...], actions=None,
  tool_choice=None, **inference_args)` returns an `AssistantMessage` whose
  `.content` or `.tool_calls` is set (`.usage` carries token counts).
  `tool_choice` takes `"auto"` (default), `"none"`, `"required"` or
  `{"type": "function", "name": ...}`; whether the deployed model honours a
  forced call is up to that model.
  `.embed(model=..., inputs=[...], **kwargs)` returns one vector per input, in
  order. `.embedding_models` lists the allowed embedding models. Calls must
  satisfy `framework/deployment_manifest.json`: a fixed value is applied for
  you (passing a different one is an error), and a constraint of the form
  `{"one_of": [...]}` is a choice you pass on every call. Embedding calls
  take no extra arguments.
- `runtime_config`: `{"company": "Redwood Inference", "role": "billing_support"}`.
- `billing`: Redwood's billing console (see "Billing console"), also
  available to tools as `self.billing`.

Anything workspace code prints goes to the agent's log, not to the developer.

## The turn interface

- `get_init_state(message_history=None) -> state` — called once per case with
  the agent's fixed greeting, `"Hi! How can I help you today?"`, as the first
  message of `message_history`.
- `generate_next_message(message, state) -> (AssistantMessage, state)` — called
  with each developer `UserMessage`, and with a `ToolMessage` (or a
  `MultiToolMessage`, `.tool_messages`) after each round of tool calls. Tool
  results are JSON text in `.content`; a failed call has `.error == True`.

An `AssistantMessage` carries text for the developer or tool calls, never both.
`ModelGateway.generate` drops narration that accompanies tool calls, so a
message returned straight from the gateway is always valid.

`workspace/tools.py` defines `class Tools(ToolKitBase)`. Every method decorated
with `@is_tool(...)` is an action: its name is the method name, its description
the docstring summary, and its parameters come from the type hints and the
docstring's `Args:` section. A tool that raises returns a failed tool result to
the agent instead of ending the case.

```python
from redwood_kit.toolkit import ToolKitBase, ToolType, is_tool

class Tools(ToolKitBase):
    @is_tool(ToolType.READ)
    def example(self, query: str) -> dict:
        """One-line description the model sees.

        Args:
            query: What the model should pass.
        """
        ...
```

## Retrieval and file fetch

Choose the knowledge representation and retrieval workflow. The kit does not
chunk or search for you. The index is a LanceDB table: vector search, text
search, or both. The support agent answers from the chunks that search
returns. Do not store full source records for a later read. Exact billing
rules stay in those retrieved chunks. Ship all runtime knowledge in the
read-only workspace; the support agent cannot access `/app/R`.

LanceDB is installed. Put gateway vectors and the source text in one table,
then build a full-text index on that text. Search with a vector, with text,
or with both:

```python
table.search(query_type="hybrid").vector(query_vector).text(query_text).limit(8).to_list()
```

Compute the stored vectors and `query_vector` with `redwood_kit.embeddings.embed`

model (`sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, 384 dimensions, CPU; no API key).
It reads at most 256 tokens (about 1,000 characters) per text and ignores the
rest, and embeds roughly 28 such texts per second on this container. Pass the
texts in one call; it batches internally. Do not use LanceDB's own embedding
functions. Use the model in the deployment manifest for document and query
vectors. NumPy is installed.

Practice questions (`framework/retrieval_probes.json`) and how to read your

=== agent.py
from pathlib import Path

from redwood_kit.agent_context import get_agent_context
from redwood_kit.messages import SystemMessage
from redwood_kit.skills import load_skills
from redwood_kit.subagents import load_subagents

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
MODEL = "openai/gpt-6-luna"


class Agent:
    def __init__(self, context):
        self.gateway = context.model_gateway
        self.tools = context.action_interface.available
        instructions = (HERE / "system_prompt.md").read_text().strip()
        for heading, name in (("Standing instructions", "AGENTS.md"),):
            if text := (HERE / name).read_text().strip():
                instructions += f"\n\n# {heading}\n\n{text}"
        if skills := load_skills(HERE):
            lines = "\n".join(f"- {skill.name}: {skill.description}" for skill in skills.values())
            instructions += f"\n\n# Skills\n\nCall load_skill with the name when one applies.\n\n{lines}"
        if subagents := load_subagents(HERE):
            lines = "\n".join(f"- {spec.name}: {spec.description}" for spec in subagents.values())
            instructions += f"\n\n# Subagents\n\nCall delegate with the name and a self-contained task.\n\n{lines}"
        self.system = SystemMessage(instructions)

    def get_init_state(self, message_history=None):
        return list(message_history or [])

    def generate_next_message(self, message, state):
        state = [*state, message]
        reply = self.gateway.generate(
            model=MODEL,
            messages=[self.system, *state],
            actions=self.tools or None,
        )
        return reply, [*state, reply]


def create_agent():
    return Agent(get_agent_context())
=== tools.py
from redwood_kit.developer import DeveloperTools
from redwood_kit.skills import SkillTools
from redwood_kit.subagents import SubagentTools
from redwood_kit.toolkit import ToolKitBase, ToolType, is_tool


class Tools(DeveloperTools, SkillTools, SubagentTools, ToolKitBase):
    @is_tool(ToolType.WRITE)
    def escalate(
        self, account_id: str, team: str, summary: str, details: dict[str, str] | None = None,
    ) -> dict:
        """Insert an escalated case record.

        Args:
            account_id: The account identifier.
            team: The receiving team.
            summary: A case summary.
            details: Named case details.
        """
        self.billing.query("accounts", {"account_id": account_id})
        case = self.billing.insert("cases", {
            "account_id": account_id,
            "team": team,
            "summary": summary,
            "details": details or {},
            "dispute_id": None,
            "status": "escalated",
        })
        return {key: case[key] for key in ("case_id", "team", "status")}

            instructions += f"\n\n# Skills\n\nCall load_skill with the name when one applies.\n\n{lines}"
        if subagents := load_subagents(HERE):
            lines = "\n".join(f"- {spec.name}: {spec.description}" for spec in subagents.values())
            instructions += f"\n\n# Subagents\n\nCall delegate with the name and a self-contained task.\n\n{lines}"
        self.system = SystemMessage(instructions)

    def get_init_state(self, message_history=None):
        return list(message_history or [])

    def generate_next_message(self, message, state):
        state = [*state, message]
        reply = self.gateway.generate(
            model=MODEL,
            messages=[self.system, *state],
            actions=self.tools or None,
        )
        return reply, [*state, reply]


def create_agent():
    return Agent(get_agent_context())
